name: Ahaz
title: The Wicked King Judah
summary: Ahaz, son of Jotham, reigned as king over Judah during a turbulent period marked by external threats and internal decay. He led the nation into deep spiritual crisis by introducing widespread idolatry, including sacrificing his sons in fire in the Valley of Hinnom according to Canaanite custom. During the Syro-Ephraimite war, when Aram and Israel threatened Judah, he rejected the prophet Isaiah's urging to trust in the Lord and refused to accept a divine sign. Instead, he submitted to Assyria’s king Tiglath-Pileser III and handed over treasures from the temple and royal palace as tribute—a political strategy that brought Judah into an Assyrian vassal relationship. He desecrated the Lord's temple by building pagan altars, altering the temple furnishings, and finally shutting the temple doors. His reign marks a spiritual low point in Judah’s history, but God’s faithfulness to the Davidic covenant was revealed when his son Hezekiah carried out sweeping religious reforms.

keyEvents.title: Ahaz Becomes King of Judah
keyEvents.description: Ahaz became king of Judah when he was twenty years old and reigned for sixteen years in Jerusalem. Unlike his ancestor David, he did not do what was right in the Lord's eyes.

keyEvents.title: Child Sacrifice and Idolatry
keyEvents.description: He made his sons pass through the fire according to the abominable practices of the nations whom the Lord had driven out before the Israelites. He sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on every hill and under every green tree.

keyEvents.title: The Syro-Ephraimite War
keyEvents.description: King Rezin of Aram and King Pekah of Israel marched up against Jerusalem to attack Ahaz, but they were unable to conquer it. Ahaz and his people were seized with great fear.

keyEvents.title: Isaiah's Sign – The Immanuel Prophecy
keyEvents.description: The prophet Isaiah urged Ahaz to ask for a sign from the Lord, but Ahaz refused under the guise of piety. Nevertheless, Isaiah gave the sign that a virgin would conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, which means "God with us".

keyEvents.title: Ahaz Seeks Help from Assyria
keyEvents.description: Instead of trusting in God, Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-Pileser III, king of Assyria, asking for help against his enemies. He took gold and silver from the Lord's temple and the royal treasury as tribute, but the Assyrian aid ultimately became a burden rather than a deliverance.

keyEvents.title: Desecration of the Temple
keyEvents.description: After seeing a pagan altar in Damascus, Ahaz ordered priest Uriah to build a copy of it and place it in the temple. He altered the temple's furnishings, removed decorations and equipment, and finally closed the doors of the Lord's temple.

versions.summary: Ahaz was the twelfth king of Judah and the son of Jotham. He is known as one of the most wicked kings in Judah's history, introducing idolatry, sacrificing his own son to Molech, and refusing to trust God when the kingdom was threatened by enemies. Despite the prophet Isaiah's attempts to guide him, Ahaz chose to seek help from Assyria instead of the Lord.
versions.title: The Wicked King Judah
versions.reason: [minor] The title is descriptive and precise, but could optionally include his order as king for more context. The current title still works well.; [minor] Ahaz's lifespan is given as approximately 735–715 BC. His reign was about 735–715 BC, but he was born around 752 BC (he was 20 years old when he became king). The lifespan should reflect birth to death, not just the period of reign.; [minor] Ahaz was not only a king, but also an idolater and political ally with Assyria. It may be useful to add roles such as 'idolater' or similar to more fully reflect his character.; [minor] Ahaz's wife/Hezekiah's mother is mentioned in 2 Chronicles 29:1 as Abi (Abijah), daughter of Zechariah. This relationship should be included.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. A profile on Ahaz should contain historical, archaeological, and theological footnotes, for example regarding the Syro-Ephraimite War, the Immanuel prophecy, Tiglath-Pileser's inscriptions, and Ahaz's signet ring which has been found archaeologically.; [minor] The summary describes Ahaz as 'the twelfth king of Judah', but the exact order varies slightly depending on whether co-regents are counted. Traditionally he is often considered the eleventh or twelfth. It may be safer to say 'one of the kings of Judah' or verify the exact number.

versions.summary: Ahab was king of Judah and the son of Jotham. He is known as one of the most wicked kings in Judah's history. He introduced widespread idolatry, had his sons pass through the fire in the Valley of Hinnom, and refused to trust God when the kingdom was threatened by enemies during the Syro-Ephraimite War. Despite the prophet Isaiah's attempts to guide him and the offer of a divine sign, Ahab chose to seek help from Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria instead of the Lord. He desecrated the temple in Jerusalem by introducing pagan altars and eventually shutting the temple doors. His reign represents a low point in Judah's spiritual history, but was followed by extensive reforms under his son Hezekiah.
versions.title: The Wicked King Judah
versions.reason: [major] Ahaz's wife is called Abi (or Abijah) in 2 Kgs 18:2, but her full name was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah. The ID should be 'abija' or 'abi' – but the most important thing is consistency. 'Abi' can be accepted as a short form, but it should be verified that this ID actually exists in the system. In 2 Chr 29:1 she is called Abijah. Both forms are acceptable, but 'abi' is a valid abbreviated form.; [minor] The phrasing "had his sons pass through the fire" is used in the summary, but 2 Kgs 16:3 mentions "his son" (singular), while 2 Chr 28:3 uses "his sons" (plural). The summary should either specify this difference or use a more neutral formulation.; [minor] The roles could be expanded with, for example, "vassal" or "tribute-payer to Assyria" to reflect his political role, even though the current roles are acceptable.; [minor] The description uses "a young woman" for the Hebrew 'almah' in Isa 7:14. This is a theologically loaded translation choice. The Hebrew word 'almah' can mean "young woman" or "virgin". To avoid taking a stance on a specific translation tradition, the phrasing could be adjusted to "a virgin/young woman" or simply render the prophecy without specifying the translation.; [minor] The footnote's wording "corresponds with the biblical account" is neutral enough, but it is worth noting that the identification of "Jehoahaz of Judah" with Ahaz is not universally accepted among all scholars, even though there is a broad consensus.

footnotes.text: The Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 735–732 BC) arose when Aram (Syria), under King Rezin, and Israel, under King Pekah, tried to force Judah into a coalition against the expanding Assyrian Empire. Ahaz refused to join, leading to the invasion described in Isaiah 7 and 2 Kings 16.

Assyrian cuneiform texts from the reign of Tiglath-Pileser III mention a king called "Jehoahaz of Judah" (Ia-u-ha-zi), who paid tribute to Assyria. Most scholars identify this king with Ahaz, providing extra-biblical evidence of his vassalage to Assyria.

The name Ahaz (אָחָז) is likely a shortened form of Jehoahaz (יְהוֹאָחָז), meaning "the Lord has seized" or "the Lord holds fast." It is notable that the theophoric element (the Yahweh part) is omitted in the biblical text, which may reflect the authors' negative assessment of his reign.

The Immanuel prophecy in Isaiah 7:14, given in connection with Ahaz, has a double meaning in Christian tradition: an immediate fulfillment related to Isaiah's time and a final fulfillment in Jesus' birth (cf. Matt 1:23). The sign was meant to assure Ahaz of God's faithfulness, but the king's unbelief caused it also to become a word of judgment.

In 2 Chronicles 28:3, Ahaz is described as one who "made his sons pass through the fire in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom." The Hinnom Valley (Ge-Hinnom) south of Jerusalem was later used as a metaphor for judgment and punishment and is the origin of the Greek word Gehenna, which refers to hell in the New Testament.

A bulla (seal impression) that may have belonged to Ahaz has been found in archaeological excavations. The inscription reads "Belonging to Ahaz (son of) Jotham, king of Judah," although the authenticity of this find has been debated among scholars.
Rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Sanhedrin 103b) counts Ahaz among the kings who have no share in the world to come, because of his extensive idolatry and his role in leading the people away from God.
